newsitem.title: FRANCE: If Buba jumps, BoF likely to follow - economists.
newsitem.headline: If Buba jumps, BoF likely to follow - economists.

text.p: The last thing France needs now is an interest rate rise, but if Germany's Bundesbank tightens, the Bank of France will have to follow, economists said on Thursday.

France's economy is beset by record unemployment and uncertain growth prospects. By raising borrowing costs just when investment and consumer confidence are starting to show signs of picking up, a rate hike could threaten the economy's fragile recovery.
An interest rate increase would be anathema to France's new left-wing government which is counting on a consumer-led recovery to pull the economy out of the doldrums.
But France's central bank may have no choice.
"I think the Bank of France would have a real problem ignoring a Bundesbank move," said Nick Stephens, head of financial markets at Credit Lyonnais Rouse Paris.

But he was not convinced the Bundesbank would decide to signal higher rates in the near-term. The German central bank sparked speculation that interest rates could move higher when it left its options open for the second part of its summer break by not announcing repos for that period in advance.

The next German repo tender is on August 12, when the Bundesbank could set a variable rate. The main argument in favour of a move to higher rates comes from the mark which has fallen to six-year lows against the dollar in recent trading.
Stephens said he thought the Bank of France might wait a week after any German move to give a semblance of independence but that market pressures would eventually force them to act.
"At the end of the day, the markets will surrogately move and money market rates will spike higher," he said.
France's intervention rate stands at 3.10 percent while Germany's repo rate is at 3.00 percent. Traditionally, the Bank of France has kept a small premium over German rates, to shelter the franc.
Some analysts said that if the Bundesbank tightens its repo rate by around 10 basis points, the Bank of France would have some room to manoeuvre. It could just sit back and accept parity.

"It all depends on the mark/franc rate. If it stays in the 3.37 zone, then the Bank of France can allow the premium to go to zero," said Marie Owens Thomsen of BIP, but she added that she thought the Bundesbank would be forced to tighten by more than just 10 basis points.

"The Germans could raise by between 30 and 50 basis points by the end of the year. If the exchange rate stays at around 3.37 (francs to the mark), then France could perhaps do 10 basis points less," BIP's Owens Thomsen said.
The franc was trading around 3.3737 to the mark on Thursday.
Some analysts said economic fundamentals argued against a matching move in France, but they added that eventually, the Bank of France would have to dance to the Bundesbank's tune.

"They can hold out. On any fundamental grounds you could possibly name, France should not have to raise interest rates, and the currency could weaken a little against the mark without triggering a run on it," said Sonja Gibbs, senior bond analyst at Nomura in London.
She said she felt that France could hold its ground for between three and six months after a Bundesbank tightening of five to 10 basis points.
"Obviously, the economic conditions are not there for a rate rise here. We have a recovery that is mainly led by external demand with no pressure on prices," said Valerie Plagnol of CCF.
She said that with the key decision on membership of a European single currency due to be made next year, European central banks would wait until then to make any adjustments to interest rates.
French markets are already pricing in higher rates. Implied three-month interest rates for September stand at around 3.54 percent compared with 3.37 percent on the cash market.
